title: The Black Death
summary: Between 1346 and 1353 a plague pandemic swept Europe. It was one of the most fatal in human history, killing up to 50 million people: 30 to 60 percent of Europe's population, and about a third of the Middle East's. The cause was a bacterium, Yersinia pestis.
kidSummary: The Black Death was a terrible disease that spread from town to town in the 1340s. In many places it killed about half the people.

views.name: From the Black Sea
views.text: Caffa, in Crimea, was a Genoese trading port. In 1347 it was under siege by the Golden Horde army of Jani Beg, and the pandemic was reportedly first introduced to Europe during that siege. As the disease took hold, Genoese traders fled across the Black Sea.
views.kid: The sickness is said to have reached Europe from a trading port on the Black Sea called Caffa. Traders fleeing by ship carried it with them.

views.name: From Italy
views.text: Galleys from Caffa reached Genoa and Venice in January 1348. Florence had between 110,000 and 120,000 inhabitants in 1338; in 1351 it had 50,000. Its tax records suggest most of its people died within four months of 1348.
views.kid: Ships brought the plague to Italy in 1348. The city of Florence lost more than half of its people.

views.name: From England and the north
views.text: From Italy the disease struck France, Spain, Portugal and England by June 1348, then moved through Germany, Scotland and Scandinavia between 1348 and 1350. About 62,000 Londoners may have died. In 1349 a ship landed at Askøy in Norway, and the plague spread to Bergen.
views.kid: The plague reached England in the summer of 1348. In London about 62,000 people may have died. A year later a ship carried it to Norway.

views.name: From North Africa
views.text: The pandemic was not only Europe's. It spread west from Alexandria along the African coast. In April 1348 a ship from Sicily infected Tunis; an army that had been besieging the city scattered and took the disease to Morocco.
views.kid: The plague also spread along the coast of North Africa. A ship from Sicily carried it to the city of Tunis in 1348.

views.name: From Egypt and Arabia
views.text: Mecca was infected in 1348 by pilgrims performing the Hajj. Four centuries later Cairo still had only half the people it had had in 1347.
views.kid: Pilgrims carried the plague to the holy city of Mecca. Cairo lost so many people that it took hundreds of years to recover.

title: The Columbian exchange
kidTitle: The great swap between two worlds
summary: From the late 15th century, plants, animals and diseases began moving between the Americas and the lands of Africa, Europe and Asia, in both directions and on a vast scale. Historians call it the Columbian exchange, after Christopher Columbus.
kidSummary: After 1492, ships began to carry plants, animals and germs across the Atlantic in both directions. Tomatoes, potatoes and maize went one way. Horses, wheat and terrible diseases went the other.

views.name: From the Caribbean
views.text: The most terrible part of the exchange was invisible. Diseases from the Old World, to which the peoples of the Americas had never been exposed, reduced the Indigenous population by 80 to 95 percent from the 15th century onwards.
views.kid: The newcomers brought germs that the people of the Americas had never met. Most of the Indigenous people died of the new diseases.

sources.title: Population history of the Indigenous peoples of the Americas

views.name: From Mexico
views.text: Maize was domesticated by Indigenous peoples in southern Mexico about 9,000 years ago, from a wild grass called teosinte. After 1492 it became one of the American crops that grew important all around the world. The word chili comes from the Nahuatl chīlli.
views.kid: Maize was first grown in Mexico about 9,000 years ago. After 1492 it travelled around the world, and so did chillies.

views.name: From the Andes
views.text: The potato was domesticated in southern Peru and north-western Bolivia 7,000 to 10,000 years ago. Carried across the ocean, it became a staple food in many parts of the world. The tomato, too, came from western South America.
views.kid: Potatoes were first grown in the mountains of Peru and Bolivia. Carried across the sea, they became one of the world's main foods.

views.name: From Ireland
views.text: A people could come to depend on a new crop too much. When the potato crop failed in Ireland between 1845 and 1852, between 775,000 and 1.5 million more people died than would have otherwise, and a million or more emigrated.
views.kid: In Ireland, many people came to depend on potatoes. When the potato crop failed in the 1840s, about a million people died and a million more left the country.

views.name: From North America
views.text: The exchange ran both ways: rice, wheat, sugar cane and livestock from the Old World became important in the New. The horse was among them, and it was a homecoming of a kind: the horse family had evolved in North America over 45 to 55 million years.
views.kid: Horses came to America with the newcomers. In a way they were coming home: the first horses of all lived in North America millions of years ago.

title: The Atlantic slave trade
summary: From the 16th century well into the 19th, slave traders shipped enslaved African people to the Americas. Most historians estimate that between 9.4 and 12.6 million people were taken. An estimated two million died at sea.
kidSummary: For more than 300 years, millions of African people were captured, put on ships and forced to work in the Americas. Many died on the way. It was one of the greatest wrongs in history.
contentNote: This record describes enslavement and the deaths of enslaved people.

views.name: From West Africa
views.text: In 1482 the Portuguese built a fortified trading post at Elmina in what is now Ghana, the first on the Gulf of Guinea. On Gorée Island, off Dakar, the House of Slaves with its Door of No Return is a memorial to the victims of the trade.
views.kid: On the coast of West Africa, traders from Europe built forts. From forts like these, captured people were put on ships and never saw their homes again.

views.name: From Brazil
views.text: The importation of enslaved Africans into Brazil began around the middle of the 16th century. Over the whole era of the Atlantic trade, Brazil imported more enslaved Africans than any other country. Slavery was abolished there on 13 May 1888.
views.kid: More enslaved Africans were taken to Brazil than to any other country. Slavery did not end there until 1888.

views.name: From the Caribbean
views.text: On 21 August 1791, in the French colony of Saint-Domingue, enslaved Africans rose against colonial rule. Their revolution is one of the only slave rebellions in history that led to a new state, free from slavery and ruled by people who had been enslaved.
views.kid: In 1791 the enslaved people of Saint-Domingue rose up and fought for their freedom. They won, and founded a new country: Haiti.

views.name: From Britain
views.text: In 1781 the crew of the slave ship Zong, owned by a Liverpool syndicate, killed more than 130 enslaved Africans whose lives had been insured as cargo. After eighteen years of attempts, Parliament banned the trade in the British Empire from 1 May 1807.
views.kid: British ships took part in the trade. After many attempts, Britain's Parliament banned the slave trade in 1807. That did not free the people who were already enslaved.

views.name: From the United States
views.text: Ending the trade was not ending slavery. In the United States the Thirteenth Amendment, which made slavery illegal except as punishment for a crime, was ratified on 6 December 1865.
views.kid: In the United States, slavery was made illegal in December 1865.

sources.title: Thirteenth Amendment to the United States Constitution

title: The Second World War
summary: From 1 September 1939 to 2 September 1945, nearly every country on Earth was drawn into one war. It killed an estimated 60 to 75 million people, about 3 percent of everyone then alive. Most of them were civilians.
kidSummary: The Second World War lasted six years and reached almost every country on Earth. Tens of millions of people died, and most of them were not soldiers.
contentNote: This record contains mass killing and famine.

views.name: From Poland
views.text: Germany marched into Poland on 1 September 1939. On 17 September the Soviet Union invaded from the east. The campaign was over by 6 October. Poland never formally surrendered, but the Second Polish Republic had ceased to exist.
views.kid: The war in Europe began here. Germany invaded Poland on 1 September 1939, and the Soviet Union invaded from the other side two weeks later.

views.name: From China
views.text: On 7 July 1937 Chinese and Japanese troops clashed at the Marco Polo Bridge near Beijing. The battle lasted three days; the war it opened lasted until 1945. It is often regarded as the beginning of the Second World War in Asia.
views.kid: For China the war began two years earlier than in Europe, in July 1937, with a battle at a bridge near Beijing. It lasted eight years.

views.name: From the Soviet Union
views.text: On 22 June 1941 Germany and its allies invaded the Soviet Union with more than 3.8 million troops along a front 2,900 km long: the largest and costliest military offensive in history. Leningrad was besieged for 872 days and never captured.
views.kid: In June 1941 Germany invaded the Soviet Union with millions of soldiers. The city of Leningrad was surrounded for 872 days, but it was never taken.

views.name: From the Pacific
views.text: On 7 December 1941 aircraft from Japanese carriers struck the US Pacific Fleet at Pearl Harbor, Hawaii; 2,403 Americans were killed, and the United States declared war the next day. Six months later, at Midway, all four Japanese fleet carriers in the battle were sunk.
views.kid: Japan attacked the American fleet at Pearl Harbor in Hawaii on 7 December 1941. The United States joined the war the next day.

views.name: From South-East Asia
views.text: Singapore, Britain's foremost military base and port in South-East Asia, fell to Japan after a week of fighting, from 8 to 15 February 1942. Occupation brought forced labour: the railway from Thailand into Burma was built by captured soldiers and at least 250,000 South-East Asian civilians.
views.kid: Japan captured Singapore in February 1942. Under Japanese rule, huge numbers of people in South-East Asia were forced to work, building a railway through the jungle.

views.name: From North Africa
views.text: Near a railway halt in the Egyptian desert, the British Eighth Army opened its offensive on 23 October 1942. In thirteen days the Axis army in Africa was crushed and driven out of Egypt. On 8 November American and British forces landed in French North Africa.
views.kid: In the desert of Egypt, in October 1942, a British army beat the German and Italian army in a battle that lasted thirteen days.

views.name: From India
views.text: India was not free, and it was at war. Its army grew from under 200,000 men to over 2.5 million, the largest volunteer army in history. At home, famine struck Bengal and Orissa in 1943: an estimated 800,000 to 3.8 million people died.
views.kid: India was ruled by Britain, so India was in the war too. Two and a half million Indians volunteered as soldiers. In Bengal a terrible famine killed millions of people in 1943.

sources.title: Indian Army during World War II

views.name: From occupied Europe
views.text: From 1941 to 1945 Nazi Germany and its collaborators systematically murdered around six million Jews, about two-thirds of Europe's Jewish population. Of the 1.3 million people sent to Auschwitz, 1.1 million were murdered there.
views.kid: In the lands they conquered, the Nazis murdered about six million Jewish people, and many others too. It is called the Holocaust.

title: The Cold War
summary: The Cold War was a rivalry between the United States and the Soviet Union, each with its allies: a capitalist Western Bloc and a communist Eastern Bloc. It began in the aftermath of the Second World War and ended when the Soviet Union dissolved in 1991.
kidSummary: For more than forty years the United States and the Soviet Union were rivals. They never fought each other directly, but wars were fought in other countries.

views.name: From Berlin
views.text: From 24 June 1948 to 12 May 1949 the Soviet Union blocked Western access to Berlin. On 13 August 1961 East Germany began building the Berlin Wall, a guarded concrete barrier that encircled West Berlin. It stood until 1989.
views.kid: The city of Berlin was split in two. In 1961 a wall was built around the western half, and it stood for 28 years.

views.name: From Korea
views.text: Korea had been divided in 1945 into a Soviet zone in the north and an American zone in the south. On 25 June 1950 war broke out between them. The fighting stopped on 27 July 1953. The country is still divided.
views.kid: Korea was divided into north and south. In 1950 they went to war. The fighting stopped in 1953, but Korea is still two countries.

views.name: From Cuba
views.text: From 16 to 28 October 1962 the Cold War came closer to full-scale nuclear war than at any other time. The United States had placed nuclear missiles in Britain, Italy and Turkey. The Soviet Union matched them with missiles in Cuba.
views.kid: In October 1962 the Soviet Union put nuclear missiles in Cuba, close to the United States. For thirteen days the world was very near to a nuclear war.

views.name: From Vietnam
views.text: From about 1955 to 30 April 1975 war was fought in Vietnam, Laos and Cambodia. North Vietnam was supported by the Soviet Union and China, South Vietnam by the United States and other anti-communist countries.
views.kid: A long war was fought in Vietnam for about twenty years. The Soviet Union and China helped one side, and the United States helped the other.

views.name: From the countries that chose neither side
views.text: Not everyone chose a bloc. From 18 to 24 April 1955, twenty-nine Asian and African states, most of them newly independent, met at Bandung in Indonesia. Together they represented 1.5 billion people, 54 percent of the world.
views.kid: Many countries did not want to take sides. In 1955 twenty-nine countries of Asia and Africa met in Indonesia to say so.

views.name: From Afghanistan
views.text: From December 1979 to February 1989 the Soviet Union and the Afghan communist government fought the Afghan mujahideen, who were backed by Pakistan, the United States and others.
views.kid: In 1979 the Soviet army went into Afghanistan. It fought there for nine years against Afghan fighters who were helped by other countries.

title: The Partition of India
summary: In 1947 British India was divided into two independent dominions, India and Pakistan. The boundary through Punjab and Bengal was drawn by commissions chaired by Cyril Radcliffe. Partition displaced between 12 and 20 million people along religious lines, amid large-scale violence.
kidSummary: In 1947 British India became two countries, India and Pakistan. Between 12 and 20 million people had to leave their homes, and there was terrible violence.
contentNote: This record describes mass violence and the abduction of women.

views.name: From Punjab
views.text: At independence the Punjab province was partitioned along religious lines amidst widespread violence, the Muslim-majority western portion becoming part of Pakistan. Lahore, capital of undivided Punjab, went to Pakistan, and East Punjab had to build a new capital, Chandigarh.
views.kid: The province of Punjab was cut in two. Its capital, Lahore, became part of Pakistan, so the Indian side built a new capital city.

views.name: From Bengal
views.text: Bengal was divided along the Radcliffe Line. The fertile east had produced food and raw materials for the industrial west. Partition left all the coal mines and all but two of the jute mills on the western side, and West Bengal suffered a substantial food shortage.
views.kid: Bengal was divided too. The farms ended up on one side of the border and almost all the mills on the other, and West Bengal ran short of food.

views.name: From Delhi
views.text: Kingsway Camp in north Delhi became the city's largest refugee camp, sheltering 300,000 people. On 30 January 1948 Mahatma Gandhi, aged 78, was shot dead in New Delhi.
views.kid: Hundreds of thousands of refugees arrived in Delhi and lived in camps. In January 1948 Mahatma Gandhi was shot dead in the city.

views.name: From the lives of women
views.text: It is estimated that during Partition between 75,000 and 100,000 women were kidnapped and raped. The Liaquat–Nehru Pact between India and Pakistan later provided that abducted women were to be returned.
views.kid: Partition was especially cruel to women. Many thousands were kidnapped. Later the two countries agreed that they must be allowed to return.

sources.title: Violence against women during the Partition of India
